title: Database application and secure booking lab · DBMS-F26

children: Database application and secure booking lab
Meetings 27–28. Use Python and PostgreSQL; one programming language is sufficient. Start with

, and configure PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, and PGUSER using your normal PostgreSQL environment. The starter prompts for PGPASSWORD if it is not set; do not commit credentials. The database must already contain setup.sql.
Read the starter and mark the SQL statements, parameter values, transaction boundary, and error paths.
to book Eli into Graph. Explain the composite-key protection against a repeated request.
Add a read-only list-events command and a cancellation command. For cancellation lock the same event row before changing bookings; all application writers must follow the same locking convention.
Return clear user outcomes for a missing student/event, duplicate booking, and sold-out event. Report success only after commit.
Use parameter binding for all user-supplied values. Explain why identifiers such as column names require a separate allowlist/composition mechanism.
Use a fresh fixture or record the rows created by each test. Graph has capacity 1 and starts empty. Remove only your test booking before the last-seat experiment.
Successful booking: exactly one new row, and the student appears once in the event roster.
Duplicate request: a second identical command returns “already booked” and does not create another row.
Missing student and missing event: clear error and no inserted row.
Quoted names: insert a test student through a parameterized helper using
. Verify exact storage and that unrelated rows are unaffected.

Last seat: run two processes for different students against event 104. One succeeds and one reports full; verify exactly one booking. Explain how the event-row lock serializes these writers at READ COMMITTED.
Rollback: temporarily raise an exception after INSERT but before leaving the transaction context. Verify no booking persists and no success message appears.
application, setup instructions, six-case evidence matrix, and transaction explanation.
add a unique request ID for idempotent external retries; explain why blindly retrying a committed-but-unacknowledged payment is unsafe.

This is a classroom concurrency contract: it assumes all booking writers lock the event row and event capacity is not changed concurrently outside that contract. Discuss enforcing the contract with restricted permissions or a stored routine in a production design.
